An example planning sequence
What should the first 90 days establish?
Use this as a planning framework. Timing depends on the product, market, procurement cycle and availability of people to speak with.
Days 1–30
Define where you can win
Compare a small set of segments and markets. Map buyer needs, alternatives, differentiation and the local proof required. Build an initial company and partner shortlist.
Decision: Which segment and route deserve validation?
Days 31–60
Test the route with relevant people
Prepare discovery questions, approach target accounts and potential partners, and document feedback. Refine the message, pricing assumptions and proposed pilot.
Decision: Is there a credible buyer problem and a workable route to serve it?
Days 61–90
Set up the next commercial test
Define a pilot or partner-validation brief with an owner, success criteria, support model and follow-up. Review unresolved commercial and delivery dependencies.
Decision: Proceed, narrow the scope, change the approach or stop?

Technical context and practical market work.
My background combines technology scouting at Sony, strategy and partnerships at Sony AI, and AI leadership at F&P Robotics. I apply that perspective to market selection, positioning, partner assessment and research-to-market decisions.

title: AI for internal data & workflows
content:
← Resources
Practical guide | Enterprise AI
Make AI useful inside your business.
Turn your internal knowledge and recurring processes into a focused AI pilot. Start with the work people do, the data they need and the decisions that should stay with them.Discuss your workflow ↗Get the pilot brief ↗By Dr. Justinas Mišeikis · Updated 6 October 2026 · Internal data & process design
Start with a real bottleneck
Where does work get stuck?
Employees searching for the right document. Support teams rebuilding an answer. Sales copying last year’s proposal. Operations chasing an exception. Each is a specific process to assess before choosing an AI tool.
Find the right information
Give employees answers grounded in approved internal sources, with links they can check.
Prepare the next step
Turn scattered records into a draft, comparison or recommendation for the person doing the work.
Act within agreed limits
Define which updates can be automated and which need a named person’s approval.
Four starting points
Your data. A specific task. A useful result.
Illustrative workflow designs, not claims of previous client deployments. Select a process to see what an assessment would cover.
01Internal knowledge & onboarding“Which policy applies, and where is the current procedure?”+Internal dataApproved policies, procedures, product documentation and onboarding material in SharePoint, Confluence or Google Drive.Work to supportFind the current source, assemble a short answer and link to the exact material. Flag missing or conflicting information.Human decisionThe document owner resolves conflicting policies. Access is checked for the employee asking, including restricted documents.Pilot evidenceTime to a verified answer, source accuracy and unanswered questions. Include outdated documents and access-denied cases in testing.
02Customer support & service“What happened before, and what should we do next?”+Internal dataTicket history, product manuals, known issues, service procedures and the relevant customer record in the CRM.Work to supportClassify the request, retrieve relevant troubleshooting steps, summarise prior context and draft a response with supporting evidence.Human decisionA service agent approves the reply and any warranty, refund or account change. Customer records remain scoped to the authorised account.Pilot evidenceHandling time including review, accepted drafts, repeat contacts and factual errors. Compare similar ticket types against the existing process.
03Sales proposals & RFPs“Can we answer this accurately without starting from scratch?”+Internal dataApproved proposal answers, product specifications, security documentation, price rules and CRM opportunity context.Work to supportMatch questions to approved answers, draft a response and highlight missing evidence or commitments that need an owner.Human decisionSales and subject experts approve scope, pricing and claims before anything is sent. Confidential past customer material is excluded unless permitted.Pilot evidencePreparation and review time, factual corrections, missed requirements and approval cycles. A faster draft alone is not the success measure.
04Procurement & operations“Why does this order or invoice need attention?”+Internal dataPurchase orders, invoice records, supplier terms, ERP status, approval limits and the company’s exception-handling policy.Work to supportAssemble the records, identify the mismatch, explain what evidence is missing and prepare the next action for the owner.Human decisionAn authorised employee approves exceptions, payments and supplier changes. Existing rules handle deterministic checks where appropriate.Pilot evidenceTime to resolve exceptions, incorrect escalations, rework and audit completeness. Include missing records and conflicting values.
Before selecting a platform
Map the process and the data it depends on.
For one workflow, follow a real case from its trigger to its final outcome. Include the time spent waiting, checking and correcting.
01
Trigger
What starts the work? Who owns the result?
02
Sources
Which records and documents are needed?
03
Work
What is retrieved, compared or drafted?
04
Approval
Who checks exceptions and approves actions?
05
Outcome
Where is the result recorded and measured?
What is the source of truth?
Name the data owner, authoritative version, refresh cycle and missing fields. Read changing order or account status from its system of record; use documents for explanatory context.
Who may see and change what?
Map existing user permissions to search results and actions. Define retention, hosting and logging requirements with the client’s IT and data owners before selecting a deployment approach.
Document-level access checks are an implementation requirement, not something a prompt can replace. See Microsoft’s access-control guidance for one concrete example; feature maturity and connector coverage must be checked for the chosen platform.
A bounded first pilot
One team. One process. Evidence before expansion.
Start with a representative set of completed cases that the client is authorised to use. Compare the proposed workflow with the current process, including human review and correction time.
Use the simplest approach that meets the need. Search or rules-based automation may be enough. Anthropic’s workflow guidance explains the trade-off between predictable workflows and more autonomous agents.
Agree the baseline
Record current handling time, volume, error types, escalation rate and cost per completed case.
Define pass and stop criteria
Set task-specific quality thresholds, access tests and acceptable review effort before evaluating the pilot. Include cases where the right response is to ask for help.
Test realistic failures
Use missing and outdated sources, conflicting records, unauthorised requests, misleading instructions inside documents and unavailable connected systems.
Decide what earns a rollout
Compare quality, adoption and full operating cost. Expand only after the agreed criteria are met and someone owns monitoring and exceptions.
What I help you produce
A brief your team can act on.
Opportunity & process map
A prioritised shortlist of workflows, the current steps and handoffs, and a recommendation on where to start.
Data & readiness assessment
A source and system map, ownership and permissions, integration dependencies, and gaps that need fixing.
Pilot & decision brief
A scoped workflow, evaluation cases, cost assumptions, acceptance criteria and a handoff for your internal team or implementation partner.
Make the economics explicit.
Time released = case volume × reduction in average handling time, including review and rework. Cash savings require an actual reduction in spend. Account for integration, licences, model usage, support and ongoing evaluation separately.
Reusable worksheet
Describe your first workflow.
Use the blank brief with your operations, IT and data owners. Start with the process and system names; sensitive company data is not needed for an initial conversation.
What task repeats, and who owns it?
Which systems and documents does it use?
Where is time lost or quality inconsistent?
What may AI draft, recommend or change?
What would make a pilot worth continuing?Download the pilot brief (TXT) ↓
Put the context to work
Bring one process worth improving.
I can help assess the opportunity, map the data and define a pilot with useful decision criteria. Implementation responsibilities are agreed with your team or chosen delivery partner.Discuss your workflow ↗

content:

RaaS ROI calculator.
Explore the costs of robotics as a service. Keep cash savings separate from estimated productivity value, and make the assumptions visible.
Illustrative scenario
Values are assumptions, not quotes or market benchmarks. Currency selection changes the label only; it does not convert amounts.

Cumulative position
Cash first. Value separately.Net cash positionIncluding productivity value
Cash line includes setup at month zero. Productivity value is included only at your selected realisation percentage.
First-month breakdown
Read the assumptions.
“Workers per shift” is multiplied by shifts, 8 hours per shift, working days and 4.33 weeks per month. Turnover replacement cost is assumed to be 75% of annual base pay.
Cashable labour reduction must reflect an actual reduction or avoided spend. Extra output has no cash value here unless you explicitly recognise incremental productivity value. Do not count the same output twice.
The model assumes the proposed robot fleet can support the workload. Validate capacity, ramp-up, downtime, integration, staffing and ongoing costs before making a decision. No discounting, taxes or residual value are modelled.
